section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that the simple meaning of "And these are the judgments that you shall place before them" refers to Moshe, and connects this to the Zohar's teaching about Moshe's unique level where there is no interruption between his soul and its source in Atzilus, enabling the connection between the two levels of Torah.
section.t: Now, the simple explanation of "And these are the judgments that you shall place before them" is,
that the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moshe Rabbeinu that he
(Moshe)
should place the judgments before Israel41.
And from this it is also understood regarding "When you acquire"
[for "When you acquire" is in the singular, referring to "that you shall place,"
as above in section 3],
that this refers to Moshe.
And the concept is,
it is stated in the Zohar42,
"In every place where a name is mentioned twice, a pause (ta'am) separates them,
such as Avraham, Avraham, etc.,
except for Moshe, Moshe, where no pause separates them."
And it is explained in Chassidus43,
that Avraham,
because his soul descended below,
a change occurred in it relative to its root in Atzilus44,
but not so with Moshe,
even when he was below, his source shone in revelation as it is in Atzilus,
to the extent that there is no partition or separation between them,
"no pause separates them."
And the reason for this, that even when he was below he was as he is in Atzilus,
is,
because the root of Moshe's soul is from the aspect of the Circles (Iggulim) that are above the chain of descent (Hishtalshelus),
and relative to that which is above the chain of descent,
Atzilus and Asiyah are equal45.
And this is why it was said to Moshe, "that you shall place before them, when you acquire,"
because the connection of the two levels of Torah
[as it is clothed in human intellect
("you shall place before them")
and as it is Your Torah in Atzilus
("acquisition")]
is through the revelation of that which is above the chain of descent, drawn down through Moshe.
And as explained above
(section 3)
that the connection of his Torah
(of the person)
with the Torah of Havayah,
is through the revelation of Ein Sof.

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that when a person learns Torah with the awareness that it is God's Torah, his learning is characterized by total self-nullification like a servant to a master, and his understanding of Torah through his own intellect does not contradict this nullification because it stems from God's omnipotence.
section.t: Now, the aforementioned explanation of "When you acquire,"
that it refers to "that you shall place before them,"
can be connected with the simple explanation that "When you acquire" refers to what follows,
"When you acquire a servant,"
for when his Torah study is in the manner of "When you acquire,"
that he feels that the Torah he is learning is the Torah of Havayah,
his learning is with ultimate self-nullification,
analogous to the nullification of a servant to the master.
For although the matter of learning is
(not that a person should nullify his intellect to the Torah,
but rather on the contrary)
that he should understand the Torah with his own intellect,
which matter is connected
(seemingly)
with his own sense of self-existence,
and all the more so when his learning is in a manner that the Torah is his Torah
(of the person),
nevertheless,
by means of his feeling that the Torah
(even after it descended below and became clothed in human intellect)
is the Torah of Havayah,
the wisdom of the Holy One, blessed be He, which is above the intellect of created beings,
[and that a person understands the Torah with his own intellect is because the Holy One, blessed be He, is not limited by any limitations
(not even by the definition of "without limit")
and therefore it is within His power, blessed be He, to join the opposites of "without limit" and limit46,
so that human intellect
(which is limited)
can grasp His wisdom, blessed be He
(which is unlimited)],
this that he understands the Torah with his own intellect does not contradict the matter of nullification,
because this that he understands the Torah with his own intellect
[and also that the Torah is his]
is not due to his own self-existence, but rather because the Holy One, blessed be He, is omnipotent.

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains the Sages' phrase "the yoke of Torah," clarifying that even when a person understands Torah with his own intellect, it is a yoke of nullification because the awareness that the Torah is God's Torah makes him like a servant to the Master, and the fact that the Torah was given into his hands is by the Master's will.
section.t: And based on this, the language of our Sages47
"the yoke of Torah" will be understood,
for seemingly,
since the commandment of Torah study is
(not that a person should nullify his intellect to the Torah,
but rather on the contrary)
that he should specifically understand the Torah with his own intellect

[and also the ruling that a person engaged in Torah study must do so according to his own understanding, for "the Torah is not in heaven" and "the Holy One, blessed be He, laughs and says, 'My children have defeated Me, My children have defeated Me'48"],
what is the concept of "the yoke of Torah"?
For a yoke is a matter of nullification.
And the explanation of this is
(as above),
that through the knowledge and feeling that the Torah is the Torah of Havayah
[and that it was given into the domain of the person,
"My children have defeated Me, My children have defeated Me,"
is because He, blessed be He, is omnipotent,
and therefore it is within His power, blessed be He, to give His Torah
(the Torah of Havayah)
into the domain of the person],
even this that he understands the Torah with his own intellect is in the manner of "the yoke of Torah,"
for the Torah is his Master and he is nullified to the Torah like a servant upon whom the yoke of the master is placed.
And that the Torah was given into his domain
("My children have defeated Me, My children have defeated Me"),
is because such is the will of the "Master,"
the Giver of the Torah.
the Giver of the Torah.
